title: Δεύτερα
about: Idomeneus, stung by Ajax’s taunts, challenges him to a wager, and the two are about to quarrel in earnest until Achilles stops them and tells everyone to wait for the horses. Diomedes comes in first, springs down and hands his prize to his men; Antilochus is next, having got past Menelaus by a trick, and Menelaus is close behind him, with Meriones a spear’s throw further back and Eumelus last of all, dragging his broken chariot. Achilles pities Eumelus and proposes the second prize for him, and Antilochus objects, offering to fight any man who tries to take the horse. Achilles laughs, fond of him, and gives Eumelus the breastplate of Asteropaeus instead. Menelaus, still angry, stands up with the herald’s sceptre, accuses Antilochus of hampering his horses, and asks him to swear an oath by Poseidon that he did not cheat.

sentences.t: τὸν δὲ χολωσάμενος Κρητῶν ἀγὸς ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.l: And him, enraged, the leader of the Cretans spoke to, face to face:
sentences.i: And the leader of the Cretans, enraged, spoke to him face to face:
sentences.n: The part opens at a printed paragraph, on Idomeneus, though the line does not name him: Κρητῶν ἀγός ‘leader of the Cretans’ is his stock title, and τὸν ‘him’ is Ajax, who has just rebuked him in the last part. χολωσάμενος is the aorist participle of χολόομαι ‘be enraged’ (from χόλος ‘anger’), and ἀντίον ηὔδα, ‘spoke face to face’, is the ordinary formula for a reply; ηὔδα is the imperfect of αὐδάω ‘speak’.

sentences.t:
Αἶαν νεῖκος ἄριστε κακοφραδὲς ἄλλά τε πάντα
δεύεαι Ἀργείων, ὅτι τοι νόος ἐστὶν ἀπηνής.
sentences.l:
“Ajax, best at quarrel, ill-judging one, in all else too
you fall short of the Argives, because your mind is unkind.
sentences.i: “Ajax, best at quarrelling, ill-judging man, you fall short of the Argives in everything else as well, because your mind is unkind.
sentences.n: Idomeneus speaks, and the vocative Αἶαν ‘Ajax’ is Ajax son of Oileus, named in the next paragraph. νεῖκος ἄριστε ‘best at quarrel’ puts νεῖκος ‘quarrel’ in the accusative of respect, and κακοφραδές is a compound of κακός ‘bad’ and the root of φράζομαι ‘consider, judge’, whence ‘ill-judging’. δεύεαι is the present middle of δεύομαι ‘lack, fall short of’, which takes the genitive Ἀργείων, and ἄλλά τε πάντα ‘all other things as well’ says in what he falls short. νόος ἀπηνής ‘an unkind mind’ is the reason Idomeneus gives, and ἀπηνής is the word the Odyssey also renders ‘unkind’.

sentences.t:
δεῦρό νυν ἢ τρίποδος περιδώμεθον ἠὲ λέβητος,
ἴστορα δ’ Ἀτρεΐδην Ἀγαμέμνονα θείομεν ἄμφω,
ὁππότεραι πρόσθ’ ἵπποι, ἵνα γνώῃς ἀποτίνων.
sentences.l:
Come here now, let us two wager either a tripod or a cauldron,
and as arbiter Atreus’-son Agamemnon let us set, both of us,
as to which horses are in front, that you may know, paying.”
sentences.i: Come here now, let us two wager a tripod or a cauldron, and let us both set the son of Atreus, Agamemnon, as arbiter of which horses are in front, so that you will learn by paying.”
sentences.n: Idomeneus proposes a wager. περιδώμεθον is the aorist subjunctive dual of περιδίδομαι ‘wager’ (‘let us two wager’), the genitives τρίποδος and λέβητος naming the stake, and θείομεν is the epic aorist subjunctive of τίθημι, ‘let us set’, with ἴστορα ‘arbiter’ (literally ‘one who knows’) as the object’s complement. ὁππότεραι is the Homeric spelling of ὁπότεραι ‘which of two’, in the feminine plural, although ἵπποι is masculine in form, so it is read with the teams of horses (‘which of the two teams’). ἀποτίνων is the present participle of ἀποτίνω ‘pay’: the loser pays, and so learns. ἄμφω ‘both’ means that both men agree to the arbiter.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’, ὄρνυτο δ’ αὐτίκ’ Ὀϊλῆος ταχὺς Αἴας
χωόμενος χαλεποῖσιν ἀμείψασθαι ἐπέεσσι·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and rose at once swift Ajax, son of Oileus,
incensed to answer with harsh words;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and swift Ajax, son of Oileus, started up at once, incensed, to answer with harsh words;
sentences.n: The paragraph begins on Ajax. ὄρνυτο is the unaugmented middle of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’, so ‘rouse himself, start up’. Ὀϊλῆος ταχὺς Αἴας ‘swift Ajax, son of Oileus’ is the stock phrase, translated the same way every time, with Ὀϊλῆος the epic genitive of the father’s name. χωόμενος ‘incensed’ is the participle of χώομαι, and ἀμείψασθαι is the aorist infinitive of ἀμείβομαι ‘answer’. The colon at the end does not bring in a speech, because no answer is made: Achilles cuts in.

sentences.t:
καί νύ κε δὴ προτέρω ἔτ’ ἔρις γένετ’ ἀμφοτέροισιν,
εἰ μὴ Ἀχιλλεὺς αὐτὸς ἀνίστατο καὶ φάτο μῦθον·
sentences.l:
And indeed now further still strife would have arisen for both of them,
if Achilles himself had not stood up and said a word:
sentences.i: And now the strife between the two would have gone further still, if Achilles himself had not risen and spoken:
sentences.n: A sentence contrary to fact, in the epic manner: καί νύ κε δή … γένετ’ is κε with the aorist γένετο, ‘would have come to be’, and εἰ μή ‘if … not’ with the imperfect ἀνίστατο gives what prevented it. ἔρις ‘strife’ is the quarrel between the two men (ἀμφοτέροισιν ‘for both’), and προτέρω ‘further’ is a comparative adverb. φάτο is the unaugmented imperfect of φημί (= ἔφατο), and φάτο μῦθον ‘said a word’ means he spoke; the colon leads into his speech.

sentences.t:
μηκέτι νῦν χαλεποῖσιν ἀμείβεσθον ἐπέεσσιν
Αἶαν Ἰδομενεῦ τε κακοῖς, ἐπεὶ οὐδὲ ἔοικε.
sentences.l:
“No longer now with harsh words answer each other,
Ajax and Idomeneus, with bad ones, since it is not even fitting.
sentences.i: “Do not go on now answering each other with harsh words, bad ones, Ajax and Idomeneus, since it is not even fitting.
sentences.n: Achilles speaks to the two men, as the duals show: ἀμείβεσθον is a dual imperative, ‘answer each other, you two’, with μηκέτι ‘no longer’. χαλεποῖσιν ‘harsh’ and κακοῖς ‘bad’ both go with ἐπέεσσιν ‘words’, harsh words and bad ones. ἔοικε ‘it is fitting’ is the impersonal use of ἔοικα ‘be like’, and οὐδέ here means ‘not even’.

sentences.t: καὶ δ’ ἄλλῳ νεμεσᾶτον ὅτις τοιαῦτά γε ῥέζοι.
sentences.l: And indeed at another man you two feel resentment, whoever should do such things.
sentences.i: You two feel resentment, too, at any other man who does such things.
sentences.n: καὶ δ’ ἄλλῳ ‘and indeed at another’ turns the rebuke back on the two men: they would themselves be offended by it. νεμεσᾶτον is the dual of νεμεσάω ‘feel resentment at’, which takes a dative, and ὅτις … ῥέζοι is ‘whoever might do’, the optative of a general case, from ῥέζω ‘do’. τοιαῦτά γε ‘such things, at least’ means such as they have just done.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὑμεῖς ἐν ἀγῶνι καθήμενοι εἰσοράασθε
ἵππους· οἳ δὲ τάχ’ αὐτοὶ ἐπειγόμενοι περὶ νίκης
ἐνθάδ’ ἐλεύσονται·
sentences.i: But you, seated in the gathering, watch the horses; they themselves will soon come here, straining for the victory;
sentences.n: ὑμεῖς ‘you’ and καθήμενοι are plural, not the dual of the last two units, so Achilles is now speaking to the whole company. ἐν ἀγῶνι ‘in the gathering’ is the place where the people sit to watch, not the contest. εἰσοράασθε is the open form of εἰσοράεσθε, here the imperative ‘watch’. ἐπειγόμενοι ‘straining’ is a participle of ἐπείγομαι ‘press on’, and περὶ νίκης ‘for victory’ says what they strive for; αὐτοί ‘themselves’ is emphatic, setting the horses against the watchers.

sentences.t:
τότε δὲ γνώσεσθε ἕκαστος
ἵππους Ἀργείων, οἳ δεύτεροι οἵ τε πάροιθεν.
sentences.l:
and then you will know, each one,
the horses of the Argives, which are second and which in front.”
sentences.i: and then each of you will know the Argives’ horses, which are second and which in front.”
sentences.n: τότε δὲ ‘and then’ answers τάχ’ ‘soon’ in the unit before. γνώσεσθε is the future of γιγνώσκω ‘come to know’, and ἕκαστος ‘each one’ stands in apposition to the plural subject ‘you’. οἳ δεύτεροι οἵ τε πάροιθεν ‘which are second and which in front’ is an indirect question about the order of the horses, with πάροιθεν ‘in front’ as a word of place. Achilles’ speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο, Τυδεΐδης δὲ μάλα σχεδὸν ἦλθε διώκων,
sentences.l: So he spoke, and the Tydeus’-son came very near, pursuing,
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the son of Tydeus came on very close, in pursuit,
sentences.n: The paragraph returns to the race. ὣς φάτο ‘so he spoke’ closes Achilles’ speech, and Τυδεΐδης is the patronymic ‘son of Tydeus’, Diomedes, translated the same way every time. διώκων is the participle of διώκω ‘chase, drive on’, and σχεδόν ‘near’ with μάλα ‘very’ says how close he comes, though the Greek does not say close to what.

sentences.t: μάστι δ’ αἰὲν ἔλαυνε κατωμαδόν·
sentences.l: and with the whip ever he drove, from the shoulder;
sentences.i: and he drove on with the whip always, laying it on from the shoulder;
sentences.n: μάστι is the short epic dative of μάστιξ ‘whip’ (Attic μάστιγι), and ἔλαυνε the imperfect of ἐλαύνω ‘drive’. κατωμαδόν ‘from the shoulder’ describes a swing of the whole arm; the last part has the related κατωμαδίοιο for a discus thrown from the shoulder. αἰέν is the epic form of ‘always’.

sentences.t:
οἳ δέ οἱ ἵπποι
ὑψόσ’ ἀειρέσθην ῥίμφα πρήσσοντε κέλευθον.
sentences.l:
and his two horses
lifted themselves on high, nimbly accomplishing the way.
sentences.i: and his two horses rose high as they nimbly completed the road.
sentences.n: The duals ἀειρέσθην and πρήσσοντε show that two horses are meant, the pair of Diomedes’ chariot, and οἱ ‘his’ is a dative of possession. ἀειρέσθην is the imperfect middle of ἀείρω ‘lift’, so ‘lifted themselves, rose’, the high action of a gallop. ὑψόσ’ is the adverb ‘on high’ and ῥίμφα ‘nimbly’; πρήσσω is ‘accomplish, get through’, and κέλευθον ‘road, way’.

sentences.t: αἰεὶ δ’ ἡνίοχον κονίης ῥαθάμιγγες ἔβαλλον,
sentences.l: and ever the charioteer drops of dust kept striking,
sentences.i: and drops of dust kept striking the charioteer all the time,
sentences.n: ἡνίοχον ‘charioteer’ is the driver of the chariot, Diomedes, and stands before its subject. ῥαθάμιγγες are drops or spatters, here of dust, and κονίης is the genitive of κονίη ‘dust’ (Attic κονία). ἔβαλλον is the imperfect of βάλλω ‘strike’, so ‘kept striking’, and αἰεί ‘all the time’.

sentences.t:
ἅρματα δὲ χρυσῷ πεπυκασμένα κασσιτέρῳ τε
ἵπποις ὠκυπόδεσσιν ἐπέτρεχον·
sentences.l:
and the chariot covered with gold and tin
ran close upon the swift-footed horses;
sentences.i: and the chariot, covered with gold and tin, ran close behind the swift-footed horses;
sentences.n: ἅρματα, plural in form, means the one chariot, and the verb ἐπέτρεχον is plural too. πεπυκασμένα is the perfect passive participle of πυκάζω ‘cover closely’, so the chariot’s body is ‘covered with gold and tin’. ἐπέτρεχον is the imperfect of ἐπιτρέχω ‘run upon, run after’, which takes the dative ἵπποις, and ὠκυπόδεσσιν is the epic dative plural of ὠκύπους ‘swift-footed’, translated the same way every time.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ τι πολλὴ
γίγνετ’ ἐπισσώτρων ἁρματροχιὴ κατόπισθεν
ἐν λεπτῇ κονίῃ· τὼ δὲ σπεύδοντε πετέσθην.
sentences.l:
and not at all great
was the chariot-track of the rims behind
in the fine dust; and the two, hastening, flew.
sentences.i: and the wheel-rims made not much of a track behind them in the fine dust; and the two horses flew on, hastening.
sentences.n: The picture is of a chariot so light and fast that it hardly marks the dust. ἐπισσώτρων is the genitive plural of ἐπίσσωτρον, the rim of a wheel, and ἁρματροχιή is the track that chariot wheels cut. πολλή ‘much, great’ is the predicate: ‘the track was not much’. κατόπισθεν ‘behind’ is an adverb, and λεπτῇ ‘fine’ describes the dust. τώ is the dual article used as a pronoun, ‘the two’, σπεύδοντε is a dual participle ‘hastening’, and πετέσθην the dual imperfect of πέτομαι ‘fly’.

sentences.t:
στῆ δὲ μέσῳ ἐν ἀγῶνι, πολὺς δ’ ἀνεκήκιεν ἱδρὼς
ἵππων ἔκ τε λόφων καὶ ἀπὸ στέρνοιο χαμᾶζε.
sentences.l:
He stood in the middle of the gathering, and much sweat welled up
from the horses’ necks and from the chest to the ground.
sentences.i: He halted in the middle of the gathering, and much sweat welled up from the horses’ necks and chests down to the ground.
sentences.n: The subject of στῆ ‘he stopped’ is not stated: it is Diomedes with his chariot, at the end of his run. ἀγῶνι is ‘gathering’ as before. ἀνεκήκιεν is the imperfect of ἀνακηκίω ‘well up, gush’. λόφων (‘necks’) is the plural of λόφος, the ridge of the neck, and στέρνοιο ‘chest’ is a genitive singular, and χαμᾶζε is ‘to the ground’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὸς δ’ ἐκ δίφροιο χαμαὶ θόρε παμφανόωντος,
κλῖνε δ’ ἄρα μάστιγα ποτὶ ζυγόν·
sentences.l:
And himself from the chariot to the ground leapt, the all-shining one,
and he leaned the whip against the yoke;
sentences.i: And he himself leapt from the shining chariot to the ground, and leaned the whip against the yoke;
sentences.n: The first line is word for word line 8.320, and its English is reused. αὐτός ‘he himself’ is Diomedes, as against his horses, and θόρε is the unaugmented aorist of θρῴσκω ‘leap’. παμφανόωντος ‘all-shining’ is genitive, agreeing with δίφροιο ‘chariot’. κλῖνε is the aorist of κλίνω ‘lean’, and ποτί is the epic form of πρός, so μάστιγα ποτὶ ζυγόν is ‘the whip against the yoke’.

sentences.t:
οὐδὲ μάτησεν
ἴφθιμος Σθένελος, ἀλλ’ ἐσσυμένως λάβ’ ἄεθλον,
sentences.l:
and did not hang back
mighty Sthenelus, but hurriedly took the contest-prize,
sentences.i: and mighty Sthenelus did not hang back, but in haste took the prize,
sentences.n: Sthenelus acts for Diomedes and takes charge of the prize. ἴφθιμος Σθένελος ‘mighty Sthenelus’ is the stock phrase, ἴφθιμος ‘mighty’ every time. μάτησεν is the aorist of ματέω ‘hang back, linger’, and ἐσσυμένως ‘in haste’ is the adverb of the participle ἐσσύμενος (from σεύομαι ‘rush’). The pair οὐδέ … ἀλλά is ‘did not … but’. λάβ’ is the aorist of λαμβάνω, ‘took’, and ἄεθλον is the prize of the contest, not the contest.

sentences.t:
δῶκε δ’ ἄγειν ἑτάροισιν ὑπερθύμοισι γυναῖκα
καὶ τρίποδ’ ὠτώεντα φέρειν·
sentences.l:
and gave to his high-spirited companions the woman to lead away
and the eared tripod to carry;
sentences.i: and gave the woman to his high-spirited companions to lead away and the eared tripod to carry;
sentences.n: δῶκε is the unaugmented aorist of δίδωμι ‘give’, and the infinitives ἄγειν ‘to lead away’ and φέρειν ‘to carry’ say what the companions are to do with the two prizes, the woman walking and the tripod borne. ἑτάροισιν ὑπερθύμοισι ‘to his high-spirited companions’, with ὑπέρθυμος ‘high-spirited’ translated the same way each time. ὠτώεντα ‘eared’ describes a tripod with ear-shaped handles.

sentences.t: ὃ δ’ ἔλυεν ὑφ’ ἵππους.
sentences.l: and he unyoked the horses.
sentences.i: and he unyoked the horses.
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ ‘but he’ is either Sthenelus, the subject of the last clause, or Diomedes, who has stepped down; the Greek does not say which, and the English leaves it open. ἔλυεν ὑφ’ ἵππους reads literally ‘was loosing under the horses’, and means that he unyoked them; the Greek does not name the yoke or harness that is loosed. The unit closes the paragraph on Diomedes’ arrival.

sentences.t:
τῷ δ’ ἄρ’ ἐπ’ Ἀντίλοχος Νηλήϊος ἤλασεν ἵππους
κέρδεσιν, οὔ τι τάχει γε, παραφθάμενος Μενέλαον·
sentences.l:
And after him Antilochus the Neleian drove his horses
by cunning ways, not at all by speed, having got ahead of Menelaus;
sentences.i: After him Antilochus, of Neleus’ line, drove his horses, having got ahead of Menelaus by cunning ways, not at all by speed;
sentences.n: A new paragraph brings in the second driver. τῷ δ’ ἄρ’ ἐπ’ is ‘and after him’, ἐπ’ being the preverb of ἤλασεν ‘drove’, split from it (tmesis), and τῷ is Diomedes. Νηλήϊος ‘Neleian’ is an adjective from Νηλεύς ‘Neleus’, Nestor’s father, so Antilochus is called of Neleus’ line. κέρδεσιν ‘by cunning ways’ and τάχει ‘by speed’ are datives of means: he got ahead by his tricks, not by faster horses. παραφθάμενος is the aorist participle of παραφθάνω ‘get ahead of’, with the accusative Μενέλαον.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ καὶ ὧς Μενέλαος ἔχ’ ἐγγύθεν ὠκέας ἵππους.
sentences.l: but even so Menelaus kept his swift horses close.
sentences.i: but even so Menelaus kept his swift horses close.
sentences.n: ἀλλὰ καὶ ὧς ‘but even so’ says that Menelaus is still in the race. ἔχ’ is ἔχε, the imperfect of ἔχω, elided, ‘kept’, and ἐγγύθεν ‘close by’ is an adverb. ὠκέας ‘swift’ is said of horses each time.

sentences.t:
ὅσσον δὲ τροχοῦ ἵππος ἀφίσταται, ὅς ῥα ἄνακτα
ἕλκῃσιν πεδίοιο τιταινόμενος σὺν ὄχεσφι·
sentences.l:
As far as from the wheel a horse stands off, which indeed its lord
draws over the plain, stretching himself out, with the chariot;
sentences.i: As far as a horse stands from the wheel, a horse that draws its lord over the plain with the chariot, stretching out;
sentences.n: A comparison begins here and is not finished until τόσσον ‘so far’ a few units on. ὅσσον … ἀφίσταται ‘as far as … stands off’ measures the gap between a horse and the wheel of its own chariot. ὅς ῥα … ἕλκῃσιν is a general relative with the subjunctive ἕλκῃσιν, ‘a horse that draws’; ἄνακτα ‘its lord’ is the man it draws, and τιταινόμενος is ‘stretching himself out’, a horse stretched out as it runs. ὄχεσφι is the instrumental in -φι, ‘with the chariot’.

sentences.t:
τοῦ μέν τε ψαύουσιν ἐπισσώτρου τρίχες ἄκραι
οὐραῖαι·
sentences.l:
of it touch the rim the outermost hairs,
those of the tail;
sentences.i: the tips of its tail hairs touch the rim of the wheel;
sentences.n: τοῦ ‘of it’ is the wheel, and ψαύουσιν ‘they touch’ takes the genitive ἐπισσώτρου ‘the rim’. ἄκραι ‘outermost’ and οὐραῖαι ‘of the tail’ both go with τρίχες ‘hairs’: the tips of the tail hairs. μέν τε is the epic particle of a general statement.

sentences.t:
ὃ δέ τ’ ἄγχι μάλα τρέχει, οὐδέ τι πολλὴ
χώρη μεσσηγὺς πολέος πεδίοιο θέοντος·
sentences.l:
and it runs very near, and not much
space between, as it runs over the great plain;
sentences.i: and it runs very close, with not much room between, as the horse runs over the great plain;
sentences.n: ὃ δέ ‘and it’ is most naturally the wheel, which runs very near the horse, though the Greek would also allow the horse; either way the two run very close. πολλὴ χώρη ‘much space’ is said of the gap, and μεσσηγύς ‘between’ is an adverb. θέοντος is the genitive participle of θέω ‘run’, masculine, so it goes with the ‘horse’ (ἵππος) of 517 understood, and πολέος πεδίοιο is a genitive of the space crossed, ‘over the great plain’; πολύς is ‘great’ here, as the conventions table has it for the same words at 4.244.

sentences.t:
τόσσον δὴ Μενέλαος ἀμύμονος Ἀντιλόχοιο
λείπετ’·
sentences.l:
So far, then, Menelaus from blameless Antilochus
was left behind;
sentences.i: Just so far was Menelaus left behind blameless Antilochus;
sentences.n: τόσσον ‘so far’ answers ὅσσον ‘as far as’ of the comparison: Menelaus is behind Antilochus by about as much as a horse’s tail hairs are from the rim, which is very little. Ἀντιλόχοιο is the epic genitive, and λείπετ’ is λείπετο, the imperfect passive of λείπω ‘leave’, taking the genitive of what one is left behind. ἀμύμονος ‘blameless’ is the stock epithet, translated the same way every time.

sentences.t:
ἀτὰρ τὰ πρῶτα καὶ ἐς δίσκουρα λέλειπτο,
ἀλλά μιν αἶψα κίχανεν·
sentences.l:
but at first even to a discus-throw he had been left behind,
yet quickly he came up with him;
sentences.i: though at the start he had been left behind by as much as a discus-throw, he quickly came up with him;
sentences.n: λέλειπτο is the pluperfect passive of λείπω, ‘had been left behind’, and τὰ πρῶτα ‘at first’ is an accusative of time. ἐς δίσκουρα ‘as far as a discus-throw’ names the distance, δίσκουρα being the range of a thrown discus. κίχανεν is the imperfect of κιχάνω ‘reach, come up with’. The subject is Menelaus, and μιν ‘him’ is Antilochus.

sentences.t:
ὀφέλλετο γὰρ μένος ἠῢ
ἵππου τῆς Ἀγαμεμνονέης καλλίτριχος Αἴθης·
sentences.l:
for the good might was increasing
of the mare of Agamemnon, fair-maned Aethe;
sentences.i: for the good might of Agamemnon’s mare, fair-maned Aethe, was growing;
sentences.n: ὀφέλλετο is the imperfect passive of ὀφέλλω ‘increase’, so ‘was growing’, and the clause says why Menelaus caught up. μένος ἠῢ ‘good might’ is the mare’s strength (ἠΰς is the epic ‘good’, neuter here). ἵππου τῆς … Αἴθης: ἵππος is feminine with τῆς, ‘the mare’, Ἀγαμεμνονέης is the adjective ‘Agamemnon’s’, and Αἴθη is her name, already given when Menelaus’ team was led out. καλλίτριχος ‘fair-maned’ is translated the same way every time.

sentences.t:
εἰ δέ κ’ ἔτι προτέρω γένετο δρόμος ἀμφοτέροισι,
τώ κέν μιν παρέλασσ’ οὐδ’ ἀμφήριστον ἔθηκεν.
sentences.l:
And if still further the run had been for both of them,
then he would have driven past him and not made it disputed.
sentences.i: And if the course had gone on still further for both of them, he would have driven past him and not left the race in dispute.
sentences.n: A condition contrary to fact, like the one at 490 but with the aorist in both halves: εἰ … γένετο ‘if it had come to be’, and κέν … παρέλασσ’ … ἔθηκεν ‘he would have driven past … and made’. τώ is ‘in that case’, the subject is Menelaus, and μιν ‘him’ is Antilochus. παρέλασσ’ is the aorist of παρελαύνω ‘drive past’, and ἀμφήριστον ‘disputed on both sides’ is the word of the last part, where the English is ‘left the race in dispute’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Μηριόνης θεράπων ἐῢς Ἰδομενῆος
λείπετ’ ἀγακλῆος Μενελάου δουρὸς ἐρωήν·
sentences.l:
But Meriones, the good attendant of Idomeneus,
was left behind renowned Menelaus by a spear’s throw;
sentences.i: But Meriones, Idomeneus’ good attendant, was left behind renowned Menelaus by a spear’s throw;
sentences.n: αὐτάρ ‘but’ passes to the next driver, Meriones, whose master is Idomeneus: θεράπων ‘attendant’ and ἐΰς ‘good’. ἀγακλῆος ‘renowned’ is a stock epithet. λείπετ’ is again λείπετο ‘was left behind’, with the genitive Μενελάου, and δουρὸς ἐρωήν puts ἐρωή, the ‘rush’ of a thrown spear, in the accusative of extent: by the distance a spear flies.

sentences.t:
βάρδιστοι μὲν γάρ οἱ ἔσαν καλλίτριχες ἵπποι,
ἤκιστος δ’ ἦν αὐτὸς ἐλαυνέμεν ἅρμ’ ἐν ἀγῶνι.
sentences.l:
for slowest were his fair-maned horses,
and least was he himself to drive a chariot in the gathering.
sentences.i: for his fair-maned horses were the slowest, and he himself was the least able at driving a chariot in the gathering.
sentences.n: γάρ gives the reason Meriones was left behind. βάρδιστοι ‘slowest’ and ἤκιστος ‘least’ are two superlatives, the second with the epic infinitive ἐλαυνέμεν ‘to drive’: he was worst at driving. οἱ ‘his’ is a dative of possession, ἔσαν is the old plural for ἦσαν, and καλλίτριχες ‘fair-maned’ is translated the same way every time. ἐν ἀγῶνι ‘in the gathering’ is the same ἀγών as above.

sentences.t:
υἱὸς δ’ Ἀδμήτοιο πανύστατος ἤλυθεν ἄλλων
ἕλκων ἅρματα καλὰ ἐλαύνων πρόσσοθεν ἵππους.
sentences.l:
And the son of Admetus came last of the others
dragging the fine chariot, driving the horses before him.
sentences.i: And the son of Admetus came last of all, dragging his fine chariot and driving his horses on before him.
sentences.n: The son of Admetus is Eumelus, whom the poet does not name here; in the last part he was thrown from his chariot when its yoke broke. πανύστατος ‘last of all’ takes the partitive genitive ἄλλων ‘of the others’. ἕλκων ‘dragging’ and ἐλαύνων ‘driving’: the picture is of a man pulling his chariot behind him while he drives the horses on in front, and ἅρματα, though plural in form, is the one chariot. πρόσσοθεν is an adverb, ‘in front’.

sentences.t: τὸν δὲ ἰδὼν ᾤκτειρε ποδάρκης δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς,
sentences.l: And seeing him, pitied him swift-footed, heavenly Achilles,
sentences.i: Swift-footed, heavenly Achilles pitied him when he saw him,
sentences.n: τὸν ‘him’ is Eumelus. ἰδών is the aorist participle of ὁράω ‘see’ and ᾤκτειρε the aorist of οἰκτίρω ‘pity’. ποδάρκης δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς ‘swift-footed, heavenly Achilles’ is the stock title, translated the same way every time; ποδάρκης is of uncertain make-up, probably πούς ‘foot’ with ἀρκέω ‘suffice, ward off’.

sentences.t: στὰς δ’ ἄρ’ ἐν Ἀργείοις ἔπεα πτερόεντ’ ἀγόρευε·
sentences.l: and standing among the Argives, winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: and standing among the Argives he spoke winged words:
sentences.n: στάς is the aorist participle of ἵστημι, ‘having taken his stand’, and ἐν Ἀργείοις ‘among the Argives’ says that Achilles speaks to the whole army. ἔπεα πτερόεντα ‘winged words’ is the formula for a spoken address, here with ἀγόρευε (the imperfect of ἀγορεύω ‘speak in public’) in place of the usual προσηύδα; πτερόεντ’ is elided.

sentences.t: λοῖσθος ἀνὴρ ὤριστος ἐλαύνει μώνυχας ἵππους·
sentences.l: “Last, the best man drives his solid-hoofed horses;
sentences.i: “The best man is last, driving his solid-hoofed horses;
sentences.n: Achilles speaks, and the man he means is Eumelus. ὤριστος is ὁ ἄριστος joined by crasis, so ἀνὴρ ὤριστος is ‘the best man’, and λοῖσθος ‘last’ agrees with it. μώνυχας ‘solid-hoofed’ (with an undivided hoof) is said of horses each time. The line has no connective word.
sentences.mark: Achilles proposes a prize for Eumelus

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε δή οἱ δῶμεν ἀέθλιον ὡς ἐπιεικὲς
δεύτερ’·
sentences.l:
But come now, let us give him a contest-prize, as is fitting,
second;
sentences.i: But come now, let us give him a prize, as is fitting, the second;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε δή ‘but come now’ brings in the proposal. δῶμεν is the aorist subjunctive of δίδωμι, ‘let us give’, with οἱ ‘to him’, and ἀέθλιον is the prize of a contest (the word ἄεθλον with a suffix). ὡς ἐπιεικές ‘as is fitting’ is a fixed phrase. δεύτερ’ is δεύτερα, ‘second’, the second prize.

sentences.t: ἀτὰρ τὰ πρῶτα φερέσθω Τυδέος υἱός.
sentences.l: but the first let the son of Tydeus carry off.”
sentences.i: but let the son of Tydeus carry off the first prize.”
sentences.n: τὰ πρῶτα is the neuter plural ‘the first things’, here the first prize, which Diomedes has already won (510–513). φερέσθω is the imperative middle of φέρω ‘carry off for oneself’. Τυδέος υἱός ‘the son of Tydeus’ is the periphrasis for Diomedes, translated the same way every time. Achilles’ speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἳ δ’ ἄρα πάντες ἐπῄνεον ὡς ἐκέλευε.
sentences.l: So he spoke, and they all approved, as he ordered.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they all approved, as he ordered.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. ὣς ἔφαθ’ ‘so he spoke’ closes Achilles’ speech, and ἐπῄνεον is the imperfect of ἐπαινέω ‘approve’. ἄρα is the particle ‘then’, and ὡς ἐκέλευε is ‘as he bade’, the imperfect of κελεύω ‘order’.

sentences.t:
καί νύ κέ οἱ πόρεν ἵππον, ἐπῄνησαν γὰρ Ἀχαιοί,
εἰ μὴ ἄρ’ Ἀντίλοχος μεγαθύμου Νέστορος υἱὸς
Πηλεΐδην Ἀχιλῆα δίκῃ ἠμείψατ’ ἀναστάς·
sentences.i: And now he would have given him a horse, for the Achaeans approved, if Antilochus, son of great-hearted Nestor, had not stood up and answered Achilles, son of Peleus, rightly:
sentences.n: Another condition contrary to fact: καί νύ κέ οἱ πόρεν ‘and now he would have given him’, with εἰ μὴ ἄρ’ … ἠμείψατ’ ‘if … had not answered’ giving what stopped it. The unnamed giver is Achilles, and ἵππον ‘a horse’, with no article in the Greek, is the second prize of 538; the pronoun τήν at 553 shows that a mare is meant. πόρεν is the unaugmented aorist of πόρω ‘give’, and ἐπῄνησαν γάρ ‘for they approved’ is the aorist of ἐπαινέω. μεγαθύμου ‘great-hearted’ is the stock epithet of Nestor, Πηλεΐδην is the patronymic ‘son of Peleus’, δίκῃ ‘rightly’ is a dative of manner, and ἀναστάς is ‘having stood up’.

sentences.t:
ὦ Ἀχιλεῦ μάλα τοι κεχολώσομαι αἴ κε τελέσσῃς
τοῦτο ἔπος·
sentences.l:
“O Achilles, greatly with you shall I be angered, if you carry out
this word;
sentences.i: “Achilles, I shall be very angry with you if you carry out this word of yours;
sentences.n: Antilochus speaks. ὦ Ἀχιλεῦ is the vocative, with single λ for the metre. κεχολώσομαι is the future perfect of χολόομαι ‘be angry’ (from χόλος ‘anger’), ‘I shall be angered’. τοι can be read as σοι ‘with you’, which is how it is taken here, or as the particle ‘you see’. αἴ κε τελέσσῃς is ‘if you carry out’ (αἰ = εἰ, with κε and the subjunctive), and ἔπος ‘word’ means the proposal just made.

sentences.t:
μέλλεις γὰρ ἀφαιρήσεσθαι ἄεθλον
τὰ φρονέων ὅτι οἱ βλάβεν ἅρματα καὶ ταχέ’ ἵππω
αὐτός τ’ ἐσθλὸς ἐών·
sentences.i: for you are about to take the prize away, thinking that his chariot and his two swift horses were hampered, and that he is a good man himself;
sentences.n: γάρ gives the reason: μέλλεις with the future infinitive ἀφαιρήσεσθαι (middle, ‘take away from someone’) means ‘you are about to take the prize away’. The prize is the horse of 540, which Antilochus has won by coming second (514–516). τὰ φρονέων ‘thinking those things’ leads to ὅτι ‘that’: οἱ … βλάβεν ἅρματα καὶ ταχέ’ ἵππω ‘for him chariot and two swift horses were hampered’, with βλάβεν the aorist passive of βλάπτω in the sense ‘hinder, hamper’, a plural verb for ἅρματα, which means one chariot, and the dual ἵππω. αὐτός τ’ ἐσθλὸς ἐών ‘and he himself being good’ gives a second ground for Achilles’ pity.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὤφελεν ἀθανάτοισιν
εὔχεσθαι·
sentences.l:
but he ought to have, to the immortals,
prayed;
sentences.i: but he should have prayed to the immortals;
sentences.n: ὤφελεν is the aorist of ὀφείλω ‘owe, ought’ (not ὀφέλλω ‘increase’) used with an infinitive to say what ought to have happened and did not: ‘he ought to have prayed’. The ‘he’ is Eumelus. ἀθανάτοισιν ‘to the immortals’ is the dative with εὔχεσθαι ‘pray’.

sentences.t: τό κεν οὔ τι πανύστατος ἦλθε διώκων.
sentences.l: so he would not at all have come last of all, pursuing.
sentences.i: in that case he would not have come in last of all, racing on as he was.
sentences.n: τό is a neuter pronoun used as an adverb, ‘in that case, therefore’. τὸ κεν οὔ τι … ἦλθε ‘he would not at all have come’ is κεν with the aorist, again about what did not happen. πανύστατος ‘last of all’ is the word used of Eumelus at 532, and διώκων ‘pursuing’ is the participle of διώκω ‘chase, drive on’, as at 499, here of a driver racing after the others.

sentences.t:
εἰ δέ μιν οἰκτίρεις καί τοι φίλος ἔπλετο θυμῷ
ἔστί τοι ἐν κλισίῃ χρυσὸς πολύς, ἔστι δὲ χαλκὸς
καὶ πρόβατ’, εἰσὶ δέ τοι δμῳαὶ καὶ μώνυχες ἵπποι·
sentences.i: But if you pity him, and he is dear to you in spirit, you have much gold in your hut, and bronze, and sheep, and you have maids and solid-hoofed horses;
sentences.n: A new condition begins. οἰκτίρεις is ‘you pity’ (οἰκτίρω), with μιν ‘him’, Eumelus, and ἔπλετο is the old aorist of πέλομαι, ‘has become’, with φίλος … θυμῷ ‘dear in spirit’. The list that follows says what Achilles has in his κλισίῃ ‘hut’: χρυσός ‘gold’, χαλκός ‘bronze’, πρόβατα ‘sheep’, δμῳαί ‘maids’ and μώνυχες ἵπποι ‘solid-hoofed horses’. The conclusion of the ‘if’ is the invitation in the next unit.

sentences.t:
τῶν οἱ ἔπειτ’ ἀνελὼν δόμεναι καὶ μεῖζον ἄεθλον
ἠὲ καὶ αὐτίκα νῦν, ἵνα σ’ αἰνήσωσιν Ἀχαιοί.
sentences.l:
of these to him afterward, taking them up, give, even a greater contest-prize,
or even at once now, so that the Achaeans may praise you.
sentences.i: Take some of these and give them to him afterwards, a prize even greater, or even at once now, so that the Achaeans may praise you.
sentences.n: τῶν ‘of these’ means the goods just listed. ἀνελών is the aorist participle of ἀναιρέω ‘take up’, and δόμεναι is the Homeric infinitive of δίδωμι used as an imperative, ‘give!’, with οἱ ‘to him’. καὶ μεῖζον ἄεθλον ‘even a greater prize’ (μεῖζον is the comparative of μέγας) and ἔπειτα ‘afterwards’ give one time; ἠὲ καὶ αὐτίκα νῦν ‘or even at once now’ gives the other. ἵνα σ’ αἰνήσωσιν has ἵνα with the aorist subjunctive, ‘so that they may praise you’; αἰνέω is ‘praise’.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἐγὼ οὐ δώσω·
sentences.l: But her I will not give;
sentences.i: But her I will not give;
sentences.n: τὴν ‘her’ is the horse that is the prize, and the feminine shows that a mare is meant. δώσω is the future of δίδωμι ‘give’. The refusal is flat, and the colon passes to what Antilochus proposes in its place.

sentences.t:
περὶ δ’ αὐτῆς πειρηθήτω
ἀνδρῶν ὅς κ’ ἐθέλῃσιν ἐμοὶ χείρεσσι μάχεσθαι.
sentences.l:
and for her let him make trial
of men, whoever is willing to fight me with hands.”
sentences.i: let any man who wishes try for her by fighting me hand to hand.”
sentences.n: πειρηθήτω is the aorist passive imperative of πειράω ‘try, make trial’, and περὶ … αὐτῆς ‘for her’ names what is at stake. ἀνδρῶν ὅς κ’ ἐθέλῃσιν ‘whoever of men may be willing’ is a general relative with κε and the subjunctive. ἐμοὶ χείρεσσι μάχεσθαι ‘to fight with me with hands’ has χείρεσσι, the epic dative plural, so the challenge is to hand-to-hand fighting. Antilochus’ speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, μείδησεν δὲ ποδάρκης δῖος Ἀχιλλεὺς
χαίρων Ἀντιλόχῳ, ὅτι οἱ φίλος ἦεν ἑταῖρος·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and smiled swift-footed, heavenly Achilles,
rejoicing in Antilochus, because a dear companion was he to him;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and swift-footed, heavenly Achilles smiled, pleased with Antilochus, because he was a dear companion to him;
sentences.n: A new paragraph. μείδησεν is the aorist of μειδάω ‘smile’, and ποδάρκης δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς is the stock title of 534. χαίρων ‘rejoicing’ takes the dative Ἀντιλόχῳ, ‘in Antilochus’. ὅτι οἱ φίλος ἦεν ἑταῖρος is ‘because he was a dear companion to him’, with ἦεν = ἦν and οἱ standing for Achilles.

sentences.t: καί μιν ἀμειβόμενος ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.l: and, answering him, winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: and in answer to him spoke winged words:
sentences.n: This line is word for word the second line of 15.47–48, where a god answers a goddess; here μιν ‘him’ is Antilochus. ἀμειβόμενος ‘answering’ and ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα ‘spoke winged words’ are the formula, with προσηύδα the imperfect of προσαυδάω ‘speak to’.

sentences.t:
Ἀντίλοχ’, εἰ μὲν δή με κελεύεις οἴκοθεν ἄλλο
Εὐμήλῳ ἐπιδοῦναι, ἐγὼ δέ κε καὶ τὸ τελέσσω.
sentences.l:
“Antilochus, if indeed you bid me from home something else
to Eumelus give besides, I shall carry out even that.
sentences.i: “Antilochus, if you really bid me give Eumelus something else besides, from my own possessions, I shall do that too.
sentences.n: Achilles answers. με κελεύεις … ἐπιδοῦναι ‘you bid me give’ takes the infinitive of ἐπιδίδωμι ‘give in addition’, with ἄλλο ‘something else’ as its object and Εὐμήλῳ ‘to Eumelus’ in the dative. οἴκοθεν ‘from home’ means from his own belongings, not from the prizes of the games. ἐγὼ δέ κε καὶ τὸ τελέσσω is ‘I shall carry out that too’, with τελέσσω the aorist subjunctive used for the future. Ἀντίλοχ’ is the elided vocative.

sentences.t:
δώσω οἱ θώρηκα, τὸν Ἀστεροπαῖον ἀπηύρων
χάλκεον, ᾧ πέρι χεῦμα φαεινοῦ κασσιτέροιο
ἀμφιδεδίνηται·
sentences.i: I shall give him the breastplate that I took from Asteropaeus, the bronze one, around which a pouring of shining tin runs all round;
sentences.n: δώσω οἱ ‘I will give him’, θώρηκα ‘breastplate’, and τὸν Ἀστεροπαῖον ἀπηύρων ‘which I took from Asteropaeus’, where ἀπηύρων is a first-person form of ἀπαυράω ‘take away’, an old verb with few forms. χάλκεον ‘of bronze’ agrees with the breastplate. ᾧ πέρι is περὶ ᾧ ‘around which’, the preposition placed after its noun. χεῦμα, from χέω ‘pour’, is a pouring, and ἀμφιδεδίνηται is the perfect passive of ἀμφιδινέω ‘whirl round’: a pouring of shining tin has been made to run all round the breastplate. The exact look of this tin work, inlay or edging, is not given.

sentences.t: πολέος δέ οἱ ἄξιος ἔσται.
sentences.l: and worth much to him it will be.”
sentences.i: and it will be worth a great deal to him.”
sentences.n: πολέος … ἄξιος ἔσται is ‘it will be worth much’, with πολέος a genitive of value, and οἱ is ‘to him’, Eumelus. Achilles’ speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ἦ ῥα, καὶ Αὐτομέδοντι φίλῳ ἐκέλευσεν ἑταίρῳ
οἰσέμεναι κλισίηθεν·
sentences.l:
He spoke, and to Automedon, his dear companion, gave the order
to bring it from the hut;
sentences.i: So he said, and told his dear companion Automedon to bring it from the hut;
sentences.n: A new paragraph after the speech. ἦ ῥα, καί is ‘he spoke, and’, ἦ being the old ‘he said’, different from ὣς φάτο. κελεύω takes the dative here, Αὐτομέδοντι φίλῳ ἑταίρῳ ‘his dear companion Automedon’. οἰσέμεναι is the epic future infinitive of φέρω, ‘to bring’ (the Greek does not name what is to be brought; the breastplate is meant), and κλισίηθεν is ‘from the hut’, with the suffix -θεν ‘from’.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ᾤχετο καί οἱ ἔνεικεν,
Εὐμήλῳ δ’ ἐν χερσὶ τίθει·
sentences.l:
and he went off and brought it to him,
and into Eumelus’ hands he put it;
sentences.i: and Automedon went off and brought it to him, and Achilles put it into Eumelus’ hands;
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ ‘and he’ is Automedon; ᾤχετο is the imperfect of οἴχομαι ‘go off’, and ἔνεικεν is the aorist of φέρω, ‘brought’, with οἱ ‘to him’, Achilles. At Εὐμήλῳ δ’ the subject changes to Achilles, who puts the breastplate in Eumelus’ hands: τίθει is the imperfect of τίθημι, and ἐν χερσί ‘in the hands’.

sentences.t: ὃ δὲ δέξατο χαίρων.
sentences.l: and he received it, rejoicing.
sentences.i: and he took it, rejoicing.
sentences.n: ὃ δέ ‘and he’ is Eumelus. δέξατο is the aorist of δέχομαι ‘receive’, and χαίρων ‘rejoicing’ is the participle of χαίρω. The paragraph ends on Eumelus’ gladness.

sentences.t:
τοῖσι δὲ καὶ Μενέλαος ἀνίστατο θυμὸν ἀχεύων
Ἀντιλόχῳ ἄμοτον κεχολωμένος·
sentences.l:
And among them also Menelaus stood up, grieving in spirit,
unceasingly angered with Antilochus;
sentences.i: And among them Menelaus also stood up, grieving at heart, angry with Antilochus without ceasing;
sentences.n: A new paragraph begins the next dispute. τοῖσι ‘among them’ is the assembled Argives, and ἀνίστατο ‘stood up’ is the word used of Achilles at 491. θυμὸν ἀχεύων ‘grieving at heart’ has the accusative of respect, and κεχολωμένος is the perfect participle of χολόομαι, ‘angered’, with the dative Ἀντιλόχῳ. ἄμοτον is an adverb whose sense is not known; ‘without ceasing’ is the traditional guess.

sentences.t:
ἐν δ’ ἄρα κῆρυξ
χειρὶ σκῆπτρον ἔθηκε, σιωπῆσαί τε κέλευσεν
Ἀργείους·
sentences.i: and the herald put the sceptre in his hand and told the Argives to be silent;
sentences.n: ἐν … ἔθηκε is ‘put in’ with the preposition split from the verb (tmesis), and χειρί ‘in his hand’ has no possessive in Greek; the hand is Menelaus’. The herald’s act, and his call for silence, mark Menelaus as about to speak formally. κῆρυξ is ‘herald’ and σκῆπτρον ‘sceptre’, and σιωπῆσαι is the aorist infinitive of σιωπάω ‘be silent’, after κέλευσεν, with Ἀργείους as its subject.

sentences.t: ὃ δ’ ἔπειτα μετηύδα ἰσόθεος φώς·
sentences.l: and he then spoke among them, a man equal to a god:
sentences.i: and then Menelaus, a man the equal of a god, spoke among them:
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ ἔπειτα ‘and he then’ is Menelaus, not the herald. μετηύδα is the imperfect of μεταυδάω ‘speak among’. ἰσόθεος φώς ‘a man the equal of a god’ is the stock phrase for a hero, translated the same way every time; φώς is ‘man’.

sentences.t: Ἀντίλοχε πρόσθεν πεπνυμένε ποῖον ἔρεξας.
sentences.l: “Antilochus, formerly prudent, what sort of thing did you do?
sentences.i: “Antilochus, you who were prudent before, what have you done?
sentences.n: Menelaus speaks to Antilochus. Ἀντίλοχε and πεπνυμένε are vocatives, πρόσθεν ‘before’ and πεπνυμένος ‘prudent’. ποῖον ἔρεξας is ‘what sort of thing did you do’, with ἔρεξας the aorist of ῥέζω ‘do’. The edition prints a full stop, but ποῖον makes it a question.

sentences.t:
ᾔσχυνας μὲν ἐμὴν ἀρετήν, βλάψας δέ μοι ἵππους
τοὺς σοὺς πρόσθε βαλών, οἵ τοι πολὺ χείρονες ἦσαν.
sentences.l:
You have shamed my excellence, hampering my horses
by throwing yours in front, which were much worse.
sentences.i: You have disgraced my excellence, hampering my horses by throwing yours in front of them, though yours were much worse.
sentences.n: ᾔσχυνας is the aorist of αἰσχύνω ‘shame, disgrace’, and ἀρετή ‘excellence’ is what he claims to have lost. μέν … δέ joins two charges. βλάψας is the aorist participle of βλάπτω ‘hamper’, as at 545, and τοὺς σούς ‘yours’ is the object of πρόσθε βαλών, ‘having thrown in front’, from βάλλω. οἵ τοι πολὺ χείρονες ἦσαν ‘which were much worse’ has χείρων, the comparative of κακός, and τοι ‘you know’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγετ’ Ἀργείων ἡγήτορες ἠδὲ μέδοντες
ἐς μέσον ἀμφοτέροισι δικάσσατε, μὴ δ’ ἐπ’ ἀρωγῇ,
μή ποτέ τις εἴπῃσιν Ἀχαιῶν χαλκοχιτώνων·
sentences.l:
But come, leaders and lords of the Argives,
into the middle for both of us give judgement, and not for help,
lest ever some one of the bronze-shirted Achaeans say:
sentences.i: But come, leaders and lords of the Argives, give judgement openly between us both, and not to help either side, lest any of the bronze-shirted Achaeans ever say:
sentences.n: Menelaus asks the leaders to judge. Ἀργείων ἡγήτορες ἠδὲ μέδοντες ‘leaders and lords of the Argives’ is a stock address. ἐς μέσον ‘into the middle’ means in the open, before everyone, and δικάσσατε is the aorist imperative of δικάζω ‘give judgement’, with ἀμφοτέροισι ‘for both of us’. μὴ δ’ ἐπ’ ἀρωγῇ is ‘and not for help’: ἀρωγή ‘help’, so not to help one side. μή ποτέ τις εἴπῃσιν is a negative purpose clause, ‘lest anyone ever say’, with the aorist subjunctive. Ἀχαιῶν χαλκοχιτώνων ‘the bronze-shirted Achaeans’ is a stock phrase.

sentences.t:
Ἀντίλοχον ψεύδεσσι βιησάμενος Μενέλαος
οἴχεται ἵππον ἄγων, ὅτι οἱ πολὺ χείρονες ἦσαν
ἵπποι, αὐτὸς δὲ κρείσσων ἀρετῇ τε βίῃ τε.
sentences.l:
‘Having overpowered Antilochus with lies, Menelaus
is gone leading away a horse, because to him much worse were his
horses, but he himself is better in excellence and in force.’
sentences.i: ‘Menelaus has overpowered Antilochus with lies and gone off leading away a horse, because his horses were much worse, but he himself is better in excellence and in force.’
sentences.n: These are the words Menelaus fears some Achaean will say, a quotation inside his own speech. βιησάμενος is the aorist participle of βιάομαι ‘use force on, overpower’, here with the dative ψεύδεσσι ‘by lies’, and οἴχεται ἵππον ἄγων is ‘has gone off leading a horse’. ὅτι οἱ πολὺ χείρονες ἦσαν ἵπποι is ‘because his horses were much worse’; the Greek leaves οἱ ‘his’ bare, and it is not settled whether it means Antilochus, whose horses were the worse at 572, or Menelaus; the English leaves it open too, and αὐτός ‘he himself’ is Menelaus either way. ἀρετῇ τε βίῃ τε are datives of respect, ‘in excellence and in force’.

sentences.t:
εἰ δ’ ἄγ’ ἐγὼν αὐτὸς δικάσω, καί μ’ οὔ τινά φημι
ἄλλον ἐπιπλήξειν Δαναῶν· ἰθεῖα γὰρ ἔσται.
sentences.l:
But come, I myself will give judgement, and I say no
other of the Danaans will chide me; for it will be straight.
sentences.i: But come, I will give judgement myself, and I say that no other of the Danaans will chide me; for it will be straight.
sentences.n: Menelaus offers to settle it himself. εἰ δ’ ἄγ’ ‘but come’ is an idiom and does not mean ‘if’; δικάσω is the aorist subjunctive, ‘let me give judgement’. ἐγὼν αὐτός ‘I myself’ has the epic ἐγών. φημι with οὔ … ἐπιπλήξειν means ‘I say that none will chide’, from ἐπιπλήσσω ‘chide’, and Δαναῶν is the genitive of Δαναοί ‘Danaans’. The feminine ἰθεῖα ‘straight’ has no noun in the Greek; the sense is that the judgement will be straight.

sentences.t:
Ἀντίλοχ’ εἰ δ’ ἄγε δεῦρο διοτρεφές, ἣ θέμις ἐστί,
στὰς ἵππων προπάροιθε καὶ ἅρματος, αὐτὰρ ἱμάσθλην
χερσὶν ἔχε ῥαδινήν, ᾗ περ τὸ πρόσθεν ἔλαυνες,
sentences.l:
Antilochus, come now, here, Zeus-nurtured one, as is the custom,
standing before the horses and the chariot, and the lash
in your hands hold, the slender one, with which you drove before,
sentences.i: Antilochus, come now, step up here, Zeus-nurtured one, as is the custom, and standing in front of your horses and chariot hold the slender lash in your hands, the one you drove with before,
sentences.n: Menelaus tells Antilochus how to stand for the oath. εἰ δ’ ἄγε δεῦρο ‘but come here’ and διοτρεφές ‘Zeus-nurtured one’ are a vocative address, and ἣ θέμις ἐστί is ‘as is the custom’. στάς ‘standing’ goes with προπάροιθε ‘in front of’, which takes the genitives ἵππων … καὶ ἅρματος. ἱμάσθλην is ‘lash’, ῥαδινήν ‘slender’, and ἔχε is the present imperative ‘hold’. ᾗ περ τὸ πρόσθεν ἔλαυνες is ‘with which you drove before’, the lash he used in the race.

sentences.t:
ἵππων ἁψάμενος γαιήοχον ἐννοσίγαιον
ὄμνυθι μὴ μὲν ἑκὼν τὸ ἐμὸν δόλῳ ἅρμα πεδῆσαι.
sentences.l:
having laid hold of the horses, the earth-holder, the earth-shaker,
swear that you did not willingly, by a trick, fetter my chariot.”
sentences.i: and, touching your horses, swear by the earth-holder, the earth-shaker, that you did not willingly, by a trick, hinder my chariot.”
sentences.n: The oath. ἁψάμενος is the aorist participle of ἅπτομαι ‘touch, lay hold of’, with the genitive ἵππων. ὄμνυθι is the imperative of ὄμνυμι ‘swear’, and γαιήοχον ἐννοσίγαιον ‘earth-holder, earth-shaker’ are the two epithets of Poseidon, the god sworn by, with his name left out as in the Greek; each is translated the same way every time. μὴ μὲν … πεδῆσαι is the oath form with the aorist infinitive, ‘that you did not’. ἑκών is ‘willingly’, δόλῳ ‘by a trick’, and πεδῆσαι is the aorist infinitive of πεδάω ‘fetter, bind’, used of hindering the chariot. Menelaus’ speech, and the part, end here.
